## Proof

We want to evaluate

$$L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \prod_{k=1}^{n} \frac{p_k - 1}{p_k} = \prod_{p\text{ prime}} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right).$$

**Step 1: Relate to the Riemann zeta function.**

For $\Re(s) > 1$, the Euler product gives

$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^s} = \prod_{p\text{ prime}} \frac{1}{1 - p^{-s}}.$$

Taking reciprocals,

$$\frac{1}{\zeta(s)} = \prod_{p\text{ prime}} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^s}\right).$$

**Step 2: Take $s \to 1^+$.**

The partial product in the problem is

$$P_n = \prod_{k=1}^{n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p_k}\right),$$

which equals $\prod_{p \le p_n} (1 - 1/p)$. For $s > 1$,

$$\prod_{p \le p_n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^s}\right) \ge \prod_{p \le p_n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right) = P_n,$$

since $p^s \ge p$ for $s \ge 1$, so $1/p^s \le 1/p$, hence $(1 - 1/p^s) \ge (1 - 1/p)$.

Therefore, for every $s > 1$,

$$P_n \le \prod_{p \le p_n} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^s}\right) \le \prod_{p\text{ prime}} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^s}\right) = \frac{1}{\zeta(s)}.$$

Taking $n \to \infty$ (so $L = \lim P_n$ exists as a monotone decreasing limit of positive terms):

$$L \le \frac{1}{\zeta(s)} \quad \text{for all } s > 1.$$

**Step 3: $\zeta(s) \to \infty$ as $s \to 1^+$.**

For $s > 1$,

$$\zeta(s) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^s} \ge \int_1^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^s} = \frac{1}{s-1}.$$

As $s \to 1^+$, $\frac{1}{s-1} \to \infty$, so $\zeta(s) \to \infty$, and thus $\frac{1}{\zeta(s)} \to 0$.

**Step 4: Conclude.**

Since $L \ge 0$ (as a limit of non-negative terms) and $L \le \frac{1}{\zeta(s)}$ for all $s > 1$, letting $s \to 1^+$ gives

$$0 \le L \le \lim_{s \to 1^+} \frac{1}{\zeta(s)} = 0.$$

Hence $L = 0$.

$$\boxed{\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{(2-1)(3-1)(5-1)\cdots(p_n-1)}{2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdots p_n} = 0}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
